newsitem.title: USA: Flooded Red River breaks spirits as well as dikes.
newsitem.headline: Flooded Red River breaks spirits as well as dikes.

text.p: Broken spirits and broken dikes told the tale of a community beaten down by the devastating floodwaters of the Red River.

Weeks of tireless effort were washed away on Saturday as the record-high-level river poured over miles of makeshift clay levees, inundating Grand Forks and its sister city East Grand Forks, Minn., with cold, muddy water.
"We put up a good fight, but we couldn't quite make it," East Grand Forks Mayor Lynn Stauss said as he ordered the evacuation of his city on Saturday afternoon.
Tom Powers, 42, was one of thousands forced from his residence by floodwaters in the darkness of Saturday morning. He said water was up to the door of his truck as he drove away.

"It's gonna break me. I'm done," Powers said, gazing out at the brown water that has invaded half the city. "I'm unemployed. I have no insurance. I guess one of the good things is that I didn't own the house. I rent."
In hindsight, the city stood little chance against the Red River, which rose so far, so fast that it overwhelmed hastily erected defenses in a matter of hours.
The river swelled to an alarming 53 feet on Saturday, well above flood stage at 28 feet and above the 1887 record of 50 feet.

City levees were only built to withstand river levels of 49 feet, although volunteers worked feverishly earlier this week to add a few extra feet of clay and sandbags for what they thought would be a crest at 50 feet.
But as the river surged, the National Weather Service (NWS) started to raise the predicted crest level, moving its estimate from 50.5 feet to the most recent figure of 55 feet.

The rapidly changing predictions prompted several frustrated listeners to call a local AM radio station and berate NWS officials for not having done an accurate job of forecasting the crest. Al Voelker of the NWS said the changes were due to more water coming faster than was anticipated.
With water now sitting still over half of Grand Forks, any further changes to the crest forecast will be purely academic.
"When you fight the river you can't be a winner," one somber caller to the radio station said.

Having evacuated their homes, flood-weary residents can now only wait for the water to subside. Many have fled to emergency shelters or friends' homes, and authorities said they may not be allowed to return to their houses for as long as two weeks.
Thousands of flood victims filled three cavernous airplane hangars on Saturday evening at the U.S. Air Force Base 15 miles west of downtown Grand Forks.

Hundreds of cots were laid out side by side, and weary evacuees pulled covers over their heads to gain some sense of privacy. Under the dull glare of electric lights, Red Cross volunteers scooped scalloped potatoes and spaghetti onto plastic foam plates.
Sonja Olson, a social worker from Grand Forks, was among those who sought shelter at the base.
"It doesn't seem real. It's like we're all here and we see it on the news but it doesn't seem real," she said.
Doug Herzog evacuated his Grand Forks house on Friday night amid the wail of emergency sirens. He told Reuters on Saturday that he had found cramped accommodations at a different site.
"We're staying with friends who live in a house west of town," a glum Herzog said. "There's six couples, two kids, four dogs, four cats -- all in that three-bedroom house."
